findings.title: Wrong metrics function on storage Create failure
findings.body: When d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) on line 45. This records the failed storage operation's duration into the legacy histogram instead of the storage one. The error path of Create mirrors the success path on line 48 which uses recordStorageDuration, so this looks like a copy/paste mistake. Consequence: a storage outage will be reported in legacy metrics (and not in storage metrics), making on-call dashboards misleading.

findings.title: Wrong metrics function on storage Update failure
findings.body: When d.Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) on line 129. The success path on line 132 uses recordStorageDuration, so this is inconsistent. Unified-storage update failures are reported into the legacy histogram, skewing alerting/dashboards built on those metrics.

findings.title: Delete success metric uses object name instead of kind
findings.body: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes the resource name where every other call site passes options.Kind. The error path on line 103 correctly uses options.Kind. Consequence: the storage_duration histogram gets one high-cardinality time series per deleted object name rather than one per Kind, which both breaks aggregation by Kind and risks Prometheus cardinality blow-up.

findings.title: Async legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage
findings.body: Inside the goroutine that calls d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, the result is reported via d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). It should be d.recordLegacyDuration, like the equivalent goroutines in Create (line 56), Update (line 140), and Delete (line 113). Consequence: every DeleteCollection in mode 3 inflates the storage histogram and never appears in the legacy histogram, hiding real legacy-side latency and errors.

findings.title: Delete uses bare logger for klog context, dropping kind/name/method
findings.body: ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) is used in Delete, while every other verb uses ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log) where log is enriched with kind, name and method via d.Log.WithValues(...). The local log is built on lines 95-96 but not attached to ctx. As a result, any code (including the async legacy goroutine) that pulls the logger via klog.FromContext(ctx) during a Delete will see the kind/name/method stripped, reducing observability and breaking log correlation for delete traffic specifically.

findings.title: Update now lets legacy compute the merge independently of storage
findings.body: The previous implementation read the current object from storage, called objInfo.UpdatedObject once, and passed the resulting 'updated' object to both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update. The new implementation passes the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update on line 139, so each backend will call objInfo.UpdatedObject against its own current state. If the objInfo applies a server-side merge (the normal Kubernetes pattern), the value legacy ends up with depends on what legacy already had, which in mode 3 is whatever the async legacy writes from previous operations have produced. This is a silent divergence risk between the source of truth and the 'safe measure' backup, and it is a behavior change vs. the prior mode 3 implementation that is not called out in the PR description.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight async legacy writes
findings.body: Destroy calls d.Storage.Destroy() and d.Legacy.Destroy() immediately. Create (line 50), Update (line 134), Delete (line 108), and DeleteCollection (line 161) all spawn goroutines that hold references to d.Legacy and d.Storage and may still be mid-call when Destroy runs. There is no WaitGroup, channel, or context used to coordinate. Consequence: pending legacy writes can race with teardown of the legacy store, producing panics, lost writes, or partially-flushed state on shutdown.

findings.title: Async legacy write inherits request context and is cancelled with it
findings.body: Each async legacy goroutine derives its 10s timeout from the request ctx (e.g. line 51: context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)). If the client disconnects or the request context is cancelled, the legacy write is cancelled immediately, defeating the 'safe measure' purpose: the most common failure mode (client cancellation right after a successful response) is the one that drops the backup. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background() so the backup write survives request cancellation.

findings.title: Legacy write errors are swallowed and not retried
findings.body: In Create (line 55-57), Update (line 139-141), Delete (line 112-114), and DeleteCollection (line 165-167), an error from the legacy store is only fed into a metric and otherwise discarded. There is no log line, no retry, and no mechanism to surface or replay the failure. Consequence: if the legacy store is temporarily unavailable, every successful unified write silently leaves legacy out of sync forever, with no operator-visible signal beyond the metric counter.

findings.title: Tests do not verify that legacy is called for any write
findings.body: In TestMode3_Create (line 65), TestMode3_Update (line 345), TestMode3_Delete (line 230), and TestMode3_DeleteCollection (line 284) the test asserts only on the storage-side return value. None of them wait on the async goroutine or assert that the legacy mock expectation was actually hit (e.g. with m.AssertCalled or m.AssertExpectations). If a future refactor drops the async legacy call, or if the goroutine is silently cancelled by the test's context, they would still pass. The test names also describe 'unified store only', which contradicts the mode 3 contract.

findings.title: Update goroutine measures startLegacy before defer cancel is registered
findings.body: Inside the Update goroutine (lines 134-141) the order is: create ctx/cancel, set startLegacy := time.Now(), defer cancel(). The defer is registered AFTER startLegacy is captured, so the recorded duration excludes the cancel defer registration but the other three goroutines (Create, Delete, DeleteCollection) place defer cancel() before capturing startLegacy. The captured time now includes the WithTimeoutCause call, inflating the legacy histogram for Update specifically and being inconsistent with the other verbs.
